title: A stellar fingerprint
caption: The young star IRAS 12196-6300 and its reflection nebulae, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: IRAS 12196-6300 · constellation Crux · about 2300 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: At the center of this Hubble image is IRAS 12196-6300, an emission-line star just under 2300 light-years from Earth. Hazy clouds float above and below it.

Spread into a spectrum, its light shows a rainbow of colors crossed by a pattern of bright and dark lines. Each kind of atom and molecule leaves its own set of lines, like a fingerprint, so comparing them reveals what the star is made of. In this star, the emission lines are especially prominent.

IRAS 12196-6300 is still in its infancy, under 10 million years old and, unlike the Sun, not yet burning hydrogen in its core. The hazy clouds are more evidence of its youth. They are reflection nebulae, formed when starlight bounces off a dense concentration of dust. That dust is probably material left over from the star's own formation, still lingering around it.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.64 x 1.47 arcminutes) and distance (2300 light years), the frame spans roughly 1.1 × 1 light-years. Its light set out about 2,300 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the star through a visible and a near-infrared filter. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, so part of this picture records light we could never see directly.
